title: Multi-Region Routing & Fallbacks — Product Launch Ops Brief
content:
Purpose:
This brief is an internal launch and enablement pack for the Multi-Region Routing & Fallbacks feature set (MRR). It covers core positioning, competitive talking points, target segments, sample announcement copy, SE enablement notes, a readiness checklist, and the immediate go-to-market tasks for launch week.

Executive summary:
MRR introduces deterministic routing policies and automated fallback chains across regions and capacity tiers. Customers can now define policies (latency target, cost threshold, regulatory region), automatically route requests to the optimal endpoint, and gracefully degrade to compatible model variants or cached responses when preferred capacity is unavailable.

Why this matters (customer problem):
- Global apps suffer inconsistent latency and availability when traffic crosses regions or hits capacity limits.
- Engineering teams either over-provision (costly) or build bespoke routing layers (slow to iterate, brittle).
- Regulated customers need predictable region residency and verified fallback behavior for compliance.

Core value props (short):
1) Predictable latency: route by real-time health + latency SLOs to keep 95th/99th latency within target.
2) Better unit economics: cost-aware routing reduces use of expensive capacity by routing cold or non-critical requests to lower-cost variants.
3) Resilience & compliance: deterministic fallbacks preserve region residency and provide audit trails for regional decisioning.
4) Developer experience: single API + declarative policies — no bespoke infra.

Positioning pillars (for external messaging):
- Production-first routing for global LLM apps.
- Keep inference close to users without sacrificing reliability or economics.
- Unified control plane: one policy language to manage latency, cost, and compliance across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Target audiences and use-cases:
- Platform teams (multi-tenant SaaS): ensure consistent UX worldwide without forks in infra.
- eCommerce & realtime comms (gaming, chat): keep tail latency low during peak events.
- Regulated industries (finance, health): enforce region residency while maintaining uptime.
- Enterprises with hybrid footprints using Redwood Dedicated + Private: centralized policy with local execution.

Competitive snapshot (quick notes for reps):
- Major cloud vendors: provide multi-region compute but lack inference-centric policy primitives (KV cache awareness, model-variant fallbacks, token-aware cost routing).
- LLM API providers: often single-region or simple region routing; few provide declarative fallback chains and cost-aware routing out of the box.
- Self-hosted runtimes: can implement custom routing but require engineering effort and lose observability/playbook integration.

Top-level differentiators (what to emphasize):
- Inference-aware routing (understands KV cache and prefix locality) vs generic load-balancing.
- Built-in model variant compatibility graph — automatic fallback to quantized/shorter-context variants with graceful degradation of fidelity.
- Transparent cost trade-offs surfaced in Console (estimated tokens saved, downstream cost delta).

Customer-facing messaging assets (short snippets):
- Announcement headline: "Keep inference fast and reliable everywhere — Introducing Multi-Region Routing & Fallbacks"
- Product one-liner: "Route by latency, cost, or regulation — automatically fall back to compatible models when capacity is constrained."
- Email subject lines: "New: Keep user-facing latency low across regions" / "Reduce inference costs with intelligent cross-region routing"

Sample announcement blurb (blog/social/emails):
Today we’re launching Multi-Region Routing & Fallbacks, a set of features that make global LLM applications resilient, predictable, and cost-efficient. Define policies that route requests based on latency, cost, or region; automatically fall back to compatible local variants or cached responses; and get per-route visibility into the latency and token economics that matter.

Sales & SE talk tracks (concise):
- For platform leads: "You can centralize routing policy in Redwood and avoid per-service routing glue. That reduces ops work and keeps user experience consistent across regions."
- For SRE: "MRR plugs into your existing latency SLOs; it respects namespace isolation and provides audit logs for fallbacks and region choices."
- For finance/cost owners: "We profile your traffic and show simulated unit cost reductions from routing and variant selection before you enable the policy."

SE enablement & technical notes:
- Key concepts: policy layer, latency monitors, cost profile, compatibility graph, fallback chain, audit log entry format.
- Architecturally: MRR runs in the control plane with lightweight edge agents reporting health/latency. Policies are declarative YAML and stored as versioned objects in the console.
- Integration checklist for Private/Dedicated customers: ensure edge agents can report to control plane (KMS-protected), configure egress rules, validate model variant compatibility mapping.
- Troubleshooting: how to read the fallback audit trail (Console > Routes > [route] > Fallbacks), interpreting "compatibility score" and when to pin models to avoid automatic fallback.

Enablement materials included with launch (planned):
- Product one-pager (customer-facing).
- SE playbook with step-by-step lab and runbook for configuring policies.
- Demo script: show a simulated capacity spike in region A and automatic routing to region B, plus a fallback to a quantized variant in region C with Console visibility.
- Slide deck for AE/SDR outreach with objection handling.

Launch timeline & milestones (high-level):
- Feature Beta: internal + select customers (Nov 2024) — complete.
- Public docs + blog: Jan 2025 — target.
- Enablement webinar & field training: week of Jan 20, 2025.
- GA + PR/social launch window: Feb 3–10, 2025.

Readiness checklist (must-haves before GA):
- [ ] Console UI copy + screenshots for policy editor (PM: Priya)
- [ ] SE lab + runbook published to internal docs (Owner: Evan)
- [ ] Pricing guidance & simulated cost-savings calculator (Owner: Finance liaison: Daniel)
- [ ] Legal/compliance review for regional claims (Owner: Marta)
- [ ] Marketing assets: blog draft, email templates, social stubs (Owner: Marisol)
- [ ] Support KB articles and triage playbook (Support lead assign)

Known risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Customers expect automatic fallbacks to be lossless. Mitigation: messaging must emphasize fidelity trade-offs and provide options to pin model versions.
- Risk: Metrics noise during early traffic profiles. Mitigation: human-in-the-loop can override policies; provide a "policy dry-run" mode to preview routing decisions.

Pricing & packaging guidance (field notes):
- Position MRR as included for Dedicated and Redwood Private with tiered support for advanced routing analytics. For Hosted API tier, include a generous baseline and pro add-on for audit/retention and advanced cost-simulation features.
- For renewals/upgrades: tie MRR to reserved capacity offers (bundle: reserved throughput + routing analytics) to simplify procurement conversations.

Objection handling (quick bullets):
- "We already have a CDN/traffic router": "Those systems don't understand inference semantics (cache/KV, model-variant compatibility) — Redwood routes with token-level awareness and provides actionable cost/latency tradeoffs."
- "Automatic fallbacks change model outputs": "We surface compatibility scores and let you pin fallbacks or set policy-level fidelity thresholds — fallbacks can be disabled per-route."

Immediate next steps (this doc owner + collaborators):
- Marisol: finalize blog draft and customer one-pager by Jan 6, 2025 (Confluence link + blog PR).
- Evan: finish SE lab and publish to internal playbooks by Jan 9, 2025 (JIRA: PLAT-4680).
- Priya: coordinate webinar agenda & field training content by Jan 12, 2025.
- Daniel: publish pricing band examples and run cost-simulations for 3 anchor prospects by Jan 10, 2025.

Appendix: quick demo script outline
1) Start with baseline: show single-region requests and demonstrate tail-latency spike.
2) Enable MRR policy: show the policy editor (latency target = 250ms, cost delta threshold = +20%).
3) Trigger spike: route to region B automatically and watch Console show routing change + audit log.
4) Simulate capacity exhaustion: show fallback to a compatible quantized variant and call out estimated token savings and fidelity delta.
5) Show dry-run mode and how to pin a model version to prevent fallback.

Notes: keep external messaging simple and engineering-focused — customers care about measurable latency and cost outcomes. This pack is intentionally practical: use these scripts and assets for field motions and update the doc with field feedback after the first two pilots.
